title: Checkable email priorities
abstract: Students deciding which university emails require action today need to check a priority recommendation against the message that supports it. This project develops a browser prototype in which users inspect current and quoted evidence, confirm or correct a suggestion, and undo a saved local label. A deterministic rule engine simulates the inference. Four synthetic threads and a fixed London clock make its behaviour reproducible. A baseline mode deliberately confuses an old quoted deadline with a current obligation. A revised mode distinguishes the latest message and requests review when a current deadline is missing. Three illustrated interactions show acceptance of a supported recommendation, recovery from the baseline error and an unresolved case. Twelve automated tests and browser walkthroughs verify the implemented states and controls. These checks establish the behaviour of this bounded prototype. Evaluating whether source inspection improves appropriate reliance requires a subsequent user study. The contribution is a working, inspectable interaction for checking and challenging email priorities.

page1.heading: Problem and scope
page1.text: The intended user is a student reviewing email before class. The goal is to identify action needed today while retaining responsibility for the decision. A1 identified a transfer question about stale evidence and missing personal context in email [1]. I narrowed the project to one editable label per thread. The developed browser interface, inference rules and session controls operate locally. Real mailbox access, replies and a learned model remain planned. This scope makes evidence checking and recovery observable within the available implementation.

page1.heading: Design rationale
page1.text: The Week 1 reading frame asks who initiates interaction, what is inferred, what is visible and what can be reversed [2, slide 14]. Here, selecting a thread initiates a suggestion, the rules infer whether action is due today, the source panel exposes the input, and Undo reverses a saved label. Keeping these variables separate prevents the recommendation itself from silently becoming the user's decision. The persistent all-messages list shows which local labels have actually changed.

Source inspection is placed beside the decision controls. The latest message and its received timestamp appear separately from an older quotation, so an authentic historical deadline can be checked in context. Kim et al. found less reliance on incorrect LLM responses when sources were available in objective question answering [3]. This motivates the design, while transfer to personal email urgency remains an empirical question. The panel shows the evidence used by the simulation without implying that a readable rationale proves the priority correct.

Inspection remains optional. Buçinca et al. found that cognitive forcing interventions reduced overreliance, with costs in subjective preference [4]. Requiring an inspection step for every ordinary message could add effort. The prototype therefore offers a direct route to the supporting text while preserving fast confirmation and correction. Whether this balance encourages sufficient checking is a future evaluation question.

The visual labels use text alongside colour. Needs your review is explicitly different from Can wait, because absent evidence should not imply low urgency. The list continues to show every thread while a selected message is inspected. This supports comparison and reduces the chance that an uncertain item disappears from attention. A long generated explanation was omitted to keep the original message close to the decision, although that choice may require users to interpret more of the evidence themselves.

page2.heading: Control and uncertainty
page2.text: The Week 1 account of direct manipulation emphasises visible state and reversible operations [2, slide 10]. Action today and This can wait directly edit the selected classification. The resulting label is distinguished as set by the user, and feedback states the scope of the change. Undo restores the previous session state. These controls also apply HAX Guideline 9 on efficient correction [5]. Saving a correction stores a local choice and does not retrain the rules.

When the latest message lacks a usable current deadline, the revised engine returns Needs your review and disables Confirm. The user may supply a priority or choose I am unsure, which leaves the label unsaved. This applies HAX Guideline 10 on disambiguation when uncertain [5]. Capability text identifies the rule-based simulation, following Guideline 1 [5]. A fixed confidence percentage would have implied calibration that this implementation has never measured.

page2.heading: Architecture and technical reasoning
page2.text: The browser sends a thread identifier, engine version and explicit decision to a local Python HTTP handler. The handler recomputes the recommendation before applying the choice, so a client-supplied priority cannot make an unresolved suggestion confirmable. Message fields feed the reused Lab 3 classifier, with expected test labels removed from inference inputs. Labels and undo history are held in separate cookie-keyed memory sessions. This provides a small reproducible prototype using the standard library. Closing the server clears its sessions.

page2.heading: Development and checks
page2.text: The project developed from the Lab 2 source-and-correction storyboard through the Lab 3 command-line prototype. For A2 I added a browser interface, separated current and quoted evidence visibly, and connected the existing label and undo operations to validated requests. The baseline reproduces B1's quoted-year error. Revised inference matches all four fixture labels, including an unresolved B1. Twelve tests pass, covering date handling, correction, undo, session separation and unresolved-confirm rejection. Browser walkthroughs checked the three sequences below and preserved screenshots. These are software checks and scripted choices. Participant effects on accuracy, time and effort remain unmeasured.

page2.heading: Limits and next evaluation
page2.text: The phrase rules recognise a restricted vocabulary and date format. Negation, implicit obligations and tasks completed elsewhere can defeat them. A correction persists only during the server session. A future evaluation should counterbalance supported advice, stale evidence and absent context, then measure correct acceptance, error rejection, decision time and perceived effort. Comparing source access with rationale-only advice would revisit A1's question. Real mailbox integration would additionally require consent and a clearer policy for retaining corrections when new messages arrive. The comparison should also include correct recommendations, because a design that merely encourages rejection could undermine useful advice. Source-opening behaviour should be recorded alongside decisions, with the distinction between choosing to inspect and being assigned an inspection condition kept clear. Counterbalancing order and using unseen threads would reduce practice effects. Participants should be able to stop or defer an item, matching the unresolved state already supported by the interface.

scenarios.title: Supported recommendation
scenarios.caption: Revised mode, thread A1. The user checks a current request and confirms its priority. Screenshots normal-before.jpg and normal-after.jpg record this sequence.

scenarios.title: Old evidence and recovery
scenarios.caption: Baseline mode, thread B1. A mistaken suggestion remains visible beside the user's correction. Undo restores the previous label state. Screenshots stale-before.jpg through stale-undo.jpg record the recovery.

scenarios.caption: Revised mode, thread B1. Missing current deadline triggers review. Choosing I am unsure leaves B1 unsaved. Screenshots uncertain-before.jpg and uncertain-after.jpg record these states.
